items.author: 0xLegendman
items.context: @0xLegendman (957 seguidores), en inglés, con imagen: un inversionista habría perdido más de $613K sin aprobar transacciones: $580K en USDT (TRON) y $23,4K en USDC (Solana) desde una Trezor Safe 7, y $9,5K desde Exodus, todo usado en el mismo iPhone; seed en papel offline. Pregunta abierta: ¿iPhone comprometido, falla de firmware/firma o seed expuesta? Noticia fresca (~27 min al elegirlo), 5 bookmarks y 0 respuestas; @ForecastQuant no ha respondido ni citado.
items.suggested_text:
Worth separating the pieces, because they probably don't share one explanation. The $9,500 in Exodus sat in a hot wallet: the keys live on the phone, so a compromised iPhone is enough. The Trezor part is different, since a hardware wallet only moves funds after a signature confirmed on the device itself.

That leaves a short list. Either the seed was exposed at some point (photographed, typed into an app "to verify", or created somewhere other than the device), or a signature was given earlier that the owner never read as a transfer. On TRON and Solana, tokens can be pulled through a previously granted allowance or delegate permission: one blind-signed approval weeks ago is enough, and it never looks like sending money.

Also telling: almost all of it was USDT and USDC, assets whose issuers can freeze addresses, a very different setup from $BTC kept on a signer that never touches a phone. The real question isn't whether the hardware failed, but which assumption around it did.
